text: Genetic analysis of populations of threatened snake species using RAPD markers. Snakes are a particularly threatened vertebrate taxon, with distributions of many species and populations becoming increasingly fragmented. At present, little is known about the degree of genetic differentiation that exists between isolated populations even though such information may be critical to their survival and conservation. As an example of how recently developed RAPD genetic markers can be used in conservation genetics, we present preliminary results from a study which used these DNA-based markers to assess population divergence in two threatened Canadian snakes, the black rat snake (Eluphe o. obsokta) and the eastern massasauga rattlesnake (Sistrurus c. catenatus). We present information on the levels of variation and reliability of amplification for fragments generated from five primers. We then use a recently developed analytical technique to estimate levels of nucleotide diversity within populations and sequence divergence between populations. Our results show that intrapopulation levels of divergence as estimated by the methods of Clark & Lanigan (Molecular Biology and Evolution 1993,m 1096-1111) approximate those found for mtDNA in vertebrates and that diversity between snake populations is small and non-significant when tested using randomization procedures. Thus, our study provides an example of how RAPDs can be applied to conservation genetic studies of vertebrates and suggest that the snake populations we examined have only recently become isolated and may be considered genetically equiva- lent from a conservation perspective, although this conclusion needs to be confirmed with other DNA-based markers.

In North America alone, Dodd (1987) has esti- mated that approximately 50% of species and subspecies warrant endangered or threatened status. An important threat to the future viability of many such populations is the prevalence with which historically widespread and relatively contiguous populations have recently become Correspondence: H. With their narrow habitat requirements and limited dispersal capabilities, snakes are particularly vulnerable to becoming restricted to habitat-isolated populations with little or no gene flow between them. For several reasons, conservation biology has become increasingly concerned about the potential genetic conse- quences of population reduction and isolation (Amos & Hoelzel 1992). For instance, in the absence of gene flow, genetic variability may be lost as a result of random ge- netic drift. Such loss of variability may be evident at the population level, in terms of reduced levels of polymor- phism and allelic diversity, and at the level of individuals, in terms of reduced levels of heterozygosity. While inbreeding has no direct effect on allele frequencies, it results in a significant reduction in the ob- served level of heterozygosity. Declines in genetic vari- ability within small populations are of particular rel- evance to conservation biology because: (1) lowered levels of polymorphism and allelic diversity may limit a population’s capacity to respond to selection, and (2) re- duced heterozygosity can cause individuals to accumu- late loads of deleterious alleles in homozygous form, re- sulting in reduced fitness of affected individuals and populations as a whole (Soul6 1980). Despite these concerns only relatively few studies have investigated the genetic structure of snake popula- tions (e.g. Sattler & Guttman 1976; Gartside et al. 1977; Merkle 1985; Paik & Yang 1987). The reason may be that snakes are notoriously secretive, making it difficult to obtain representative sample sizes for many species (e.g. Hedges 1989), particularly those that are rare. A key fea- ture of these studies is that they have used allozyme loci as genetic markers, which are less sensitive at detecting intraspecific variation and structure than are markers based on mitochondria1 DNA and certain types of nu- clear DNA (cf. Yet this is the level of variation which is most relevant to conserva- tion biologists concerned with the preservation of species that exist in fragmented populations. Thus, a more sensi- tive DNA-based marker system is required to determine if threatened species of snakes exist as genetically differ- entiated sub-populations. Randomly Amplified Polymorphic DNA (RAPD) markers may provide a useful technique for identifying polymorphic DNA markers which are sensitive to detect- ing genetic structure at the population level in vertebrates (Hadrys ef ul. 1992). The technique, first described by Williams et al. (1990), involves the use of single short oli- gonucleotides in a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to produce complex patterns of anonymous DNA frag- ments some of which are polymorphic between individu- als. Primers appear to be ‘universal’, with the same prim- ers detecting polymorphisms in both plants and animals (eg. Williams et al. 1990). Compared with other methods for detecting DNA polymorphisms, the technique is com- paratively inexpensive and technically straightforward. Polymorphisms are simply identified as the presence or absence of a DNA fragment on an agarose gel stained with ethidium bromide. The wide use of W D s for cultivar identification (Hu & Quiros 1991), and popula- tion level analyses (Russell et aI. 1993) in plants suggests that the technique may detect levels of variation appro- priate for analysing genetic differentiation at the popula- tion level in vertebrates such as snakes. In this paper, we describe preliminary results of our application of RAPDs to analyse population structure in two threatened species of snakes found in Canada.

The two species of snakes which were the focus of our study were the black rat snake (Eluphe o. obsoletu) and east- ern massasauga rattlesnake (Sistrurus c. catenatus). Black rat snakes range across much of the eastern half of the U.S. with the northern edge of their distribution extend- ing into southern Ontario (Conant & Collins 1991; Weller & Oldham 1989). The historic range in Ontario is thought to have extended continuously through south-westem Ontario north of Lake Erie until about 1880 when forest clearing for agriculture reached its peak in the province (Kelly 1990). Today, only three small and geographically disjunct populations remain in south-westem Ontario, each separated from all other populations by minimum of 50 km of unsuitable habitat. A fourth, relatively large, disjunct population occurs near the eastem end of Lake Ontario in southeastern Ontario (see Fig. la). It is unclear whether this population was ever contiguous with the population(s) in south-western Ontario. However, it was at one time undoubtedly part of a continuous extension of the extant New York state population to the south from which it is now separated by distance of about 120 km. The eastern massasauga rattlesnake is in serious de- cline throughout its range. It is officially considered threatened in Canada and is recommended for threatened status in the USA. Historically distributed throughout much of south-westem Ontario and continuing as far north as the north shore of Lake Huron, the species is now restricted to four separate regions of the province (Cook 1984; Weller & Oldham 1989); individuals from isolated Fig. 1 Locations ofsample populations of (a) black rat snakes; Rig Creek and Rideau Lakes and (b) massasauga rattlesnakes; Geor- gian Bay Islands National Park and Bruce Peninsula National Park in relation to other disjunct populations (filled circles) in the Great Lakes Region of southern Ontario.

populations at both the eastern and western ends of Lake Erie persist in relict habitat patches, while two additional populations persist at relatively high numbers on the eastern side of Georgian Bay (part of Lake Huron) and on the Bruce Peninsula (forming the western side of Ceor- gian Bay; see Fig. 16). The Georgian Bay and Bruce Penin- sula populations were probably contiguous until some- time in the early 1980s when southern Georgian Bay shoreline development effectively isolated them from each other (Weller & Oldham 1989). The purpose of this study is to present preliminary re- sults from our use of RAPD markers to estimate levels of genetic diversity within populations and genetic diver- gence between populations of both black rat snakes and massasauga rattlesnakes. One difficulty in using RAPDs for population level analyses has been the lack of an ana- lytical technique that takes into account the difficulty of distinguishing between heterozygotes and homozygotes for a particular fragment when estimating standard measures of divergence and variation. As a possible solu- tion, we show how the newly developed technique of Clark & Lanigan (1993), which corrects for this inability to distinguish between genotypes, can be used in combina- tion with randomization techniques to test for differentia- tion. Our conclusion is that, when used with appropriate caution, RAPDs can provide a valuable new source of easily generated markers for conservation genetic analy- ses of vertebrate populations.

We collected approximately 100 pL of blood, drawn from the caudal vein using an insulin syringe, from snakes cap- tured in the field during 1991 and 1992. Black rat snakes were sampled from the Rideau Lakes (Murphy's Point I'rovincial Park, N = 33) and the Big Creek (south of Tillsonburg, N = 10) populations (see Fig. Eastern rnassasauga rattlesnakes were sampled from eastern Georgian Bay (Beausolcili Island, Georgian Bay Islands National Park, N = 9) and the Bruce Peninsula (Bruce Pe- ninsula National Park, N = 9) populations (see Fig. 1B). Sampled blood was immediately mixed with 800 pL of lysis buffer (Seutin et al. 1991) and refrigerated until DNA extiaction.

Genomic DNA was extracted from the blood samples us- ing standard techniques (cf. Briefly, approximately 400 pL of the lysis buffer and blood solution was suspended in additional lysis buffer to a total volume of 4 mL, and rocked gently overnight at 37 "C until no clots remained. The samples were then di- gested with proteinase K, extracted hvo to three times with a 70:30 mix of phenol:chloroform, and once with chloroform. The DNA was thcn precipitated by adding 1/10 volume of 3-51 sodium acetate (pH 5.9, and two vol- umes of 100% ethanol. The D N A was then spooled out using a Pasteur pipette, washed in 70'% ethanol, and al- lowed to dry for 5 min. It was then redissolved in 0 3-1.0 mL of TE depending on the yield of DNA, and gently rocked overnight at 37 "C. The amount of DKA was then quantified using a Hoefer TKO 100 fluorometer and a test aliquot digested and the concentration and quality of the sample DNA assessed by comparison with known stand- ards of cut and uncut snake DNA. If the estimates of con- centration were inaccurate, then the samples were put back to redissolve at 37 "C and the quantification proce- dure repeated.

To generate RAPD profiles from snake DNA we used 20 ten base pair primers (Al-A20) from the Operon Tech- nologies Primer Kit A in PCR amplifications. Amplifica- tion reactions were performed in volumes of 25 pL con- taining 10 mM Tris (pH 8.3), 50 mM KCI, 2 mM MgCI,, 0.001% gelatin, 10 mM dNTP (Pharmacia), 5 p~ primer (Operon), 0.5 units of Taq DNA polymerase (Perkin Elmer Cetus), 50 ng of genomic DNA, and water. Nega- tive controls in which water was substituted for DNA were also run tu check for the possibility of contamind- tion. The reaction was overlaid with mineral oil and am- plified in a Perkin Elmer Cetus Model 480 DNA Thermal Cycler programmed for 45 cycles of 1 min at 94 "C, 1 min at 36 "C, and 2 min at 72 "C. After the final cycle, samples were held at 4 "C prior to analysis. Amplification proci- ucts were separated according to size on 1.2% agarose gels run in 0.5 x TBE, stained with 35 pL ethidium bro- mide (10 mg/mL) in 700 mL 0.5 x TBE, dcstained for 30 min in water and then visualized under ultraviolet light. Monochrome photographic negatives were taken uf the gels and the profiles of individuzls were scored by one of us (KAP) for the presence/absence of fragments for each primer by projecting the photographic negative image onto flat white screen at a standard distance of 3 m. Initially, we survcyed all 20 (Al-AZO) of the Operon primers for a sample of 20 black rat snakes and 16 (Al-A16) of these primers for 10 eastern massasauga rattlesnakes. Based on clarity and crispness of the profiles produced, we then chose four of these primers for each species which we then used to generate profiles for a larger sample of individuals. We emphasize that primers were only evaluated on the basis of how clear and easily scored the profiles were and not on the basis of the degree of fragment polymorphism [see Clark & Lanigan (1993) 1365294x, 1994, 4, Downloaded from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-294X.1994.tb00072.x by Queen'S University, Wiley Online Library on [19/02/2023]. The primers chosen were Al, A5, A7, and A20 for the black rat snakes and A4, A10, A12, and A16 for the rattle- snakes. To quantify the repeatability of the fragments produced by the four primers used for rat snakes, we ran two separate amplifications for the same 15 individuals. After blindly scoring the presence or absence of specific fragments in these 15 individuals we calculated a ‘repeat- ability’ score for each fragment based on the consistency with which a particular fragment was either present or absent in the two sets of amplifications. For example, if a particular fragment was consistently present or consist- ently absent between amplifications in all 15 individuals, then that fragment was given a repeatability score of 1.0. In contrast, if 10 of 15 individuals were scored differently for a particular fragment then the fragment would be as- signed a repeatability of 0.33. We did not estimate repeatabilities for fragments from the rattlesnake profiles.

Most population level analyses of RAPD profiles com- pleted to date have failed to incorporate any correction for the inability to discriminate between individuals who are heterozygous compared to those who are homo- zygous for a particular fragment (e.g. Kazan etal. This failure may seriously underesti- mate the level of genetic diversity detected by these mark- ers (Clark & Lanigan 1993). Recently, Clark & Lanigan (1993) have proposed a new method for estimating genetic diversity from RAPDs which corrects for the inability to discriminate between heterozygotes and homozygotes in a population sample. It uses frequency of the absence of a fragment in a popu- lation sample as an estimate of the population frequency of recessive homozygotes (i.e. q2) and then uses this value to correct for the relative ‘detectability’ of individuals who have one versus two copies of a fragment. A modi- fied band sharing coefficient (cf. Nei & Li 1979) between pairwise combinations of individuals can then be calcu- lated and used to estimate levels of nucleotide diversity within populations (P; Nei & Li 1979) and the extent of nucleotide divergence between populations (D; Nei & Miller 1990). In applying the methods of Clark & Lanigan (1993) we make the following assumptions about RAPD profiles in snakes: (1) Polymorphic bands segregate in a Mendelian fashion; (2) Same-size fragments in different individuals are allelic and have not arisen through independent mu- tational events; and (3) Single nucleotide substitutions rather than insertions and deletions are the principle cause of a lack of amplification at a particular priming site. This method also assumes that genotypes show Hardy-Weinberg proportions within populations. We are unable to test these assumptions for the snake RAPDs described here. However, studies of other organisms (cf. Williams ef al. 1990; Carlson ef al. 1991; Chalmers et al. 1992) show that assumptions 1 and 2 apply to most frag- ments and Williams et al. (1990) experimentally demon- strated that the mechanism described under assumption 3 (single base substitutions) usually leads to a loss of prim- ing sites. Clearly, however, the validity of our estimates of P and D are dependent on how well these assumptions of Clark & Lanigan’s (1993) method of analysis are met. We used the program RAPDDIP, kindly provided by A. G. Clark (Penn State University) to calculate values of P and D from the RAPD profiles generated from our snake populations. To test the significance of the value for inter- population divergence (D) we used a bootstrap random- ization procedure [see Manly (1991) for description] to generate null distributions for D which were expected if no geographic structure was present. Geographic struc- ture occurs when divergence values are higher on aver- age between individuals from different populations than those between individuals of the same population. Boot- strapped data sets were created by pooling all individuals from both populations and then randomly resampling individuals with replacement from this combined pool until both populations attained their original size. The program RAPDDIP was then used to calculate a D value for each of these null data sets and the 95th percentile of this null distribution was used to test the significance of the observed D from the original data set.

In this study we have shown that, first, RAPDs detect sub- stantial numbers of polymorphic DNA-based genetic markers within snake populations making them useful for conservation genetic studies of this taxa. Secondly, our results. suggest that populations of both black rat snakes and massasauga rattlesnakes investigated here are not strongly differentiated with respect to their RAPD genotypes.

To our knowledge, this is the first study to use DNA- based markers for conservation genetic analyses of threatened snakes. (1992) have reviewed the advantages that RAPDs have over other DNA-based markers for genetic analyses of populations including ef- ficiency and low cost, and the ability to conduct analyses on organisms for which no species-specific markers are available. Our results confirm the later advantage for snakes by showing that RAPDs detect adequate levels of variation for population level analyses in two species in this taxon. Furthermore, we have illustrated how the newly-developed methods of Clark and Lanigan (1993) for analysing RAPD data can be combined with a boot- strap test to look for evidence of significant genetic differ- entiation between isolated populations. The Clark & Lanigan (1993) approach has a number of advantages over previously described methods for quan- tifying population differences in RAPDs. First, the simple band-sharing estimates used previously (cf. 1993) pool hetero- and homozygous individuals because they exhibit the same phenotype (‘presence of a band’). This reduces the sensitivity of the technique to detect fine- scale differences between populations that are the result of different ’allele’ (eg. band) frequencies rather than the simple presence or absence of ’alleles’. However, such subtle genetic differences may be crucially important 1365294x, 1994, 4, Downloaded from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-294X.1994.tb00072.x by Queen'S University, Wiley Online Library on [19/02/2023]. See the Terms and Conditions (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/terms-and-conditions) on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License when attempting to quantify the effects of phenomena which are of interest to conservation biologists such as the effect of isolation on levels of variation in populations. The Clark & Lanigan (1993) method of quantifying RAPD variation accounts for this problem by incorporating esti- mates of the frequencies of the different genotypes into band sharing estimates. A second advantage of the Clark & Lanigan (1993) method is that it quantifies estimates of within and be- tween population variation in terms of genetic param- eters (e.g. D) which are commonly used to estimate levels of variation with other DNA-based genetic markers. Thus, estimates of genetic diversity based on a variety of markers can be compared using a common measure (nu- cleotide diversity per site) which is also an important pa- rameter in molecular evolutionary genetics theory (e.g. Nei 1987). Thus, predictions from this theory or tests of specific hypotheses about genetic phenomena derived from this theory which are of interest to conservation bi- ologists become accessible to the field when a parameter like D is used. We feel this is a distinct advantage over other measures of genetic diversity which have been ap- plied to RAPD data (e.g. Shannon's index of phenotypic diversity; Russell et al. 1993) which have no obvious rela- tionship with population genetic theory. One value of direct comparisons of estimates of the same genetic parameters using data from different types of markers is to identify those which evolve at similar rates. In this respect we are struck by the similarity of P values estimated from snake and bird populations and those estimated from intrapopulation surveys of mtDNA variation. The first evidence comes from a comparison of the values of P estimated for our two snake species (O.OOlS-O.003) with those reported by Avise et nl. for mtDNA variation in three reptiles (0.002-0.051). Clearly, differences in taxa, the small number of species surveyed, and the differences in geographic scale over which sapples were collected complicate direct compari- son of these values. Nonetheless, we note the substantial overlap in the ranges of these values. The second evidence comes from a study by Gibbs et al. (in preparation) which compared levels of intrapopulation diversity for mtDNA sequence from the control region and five RAPD markers for a sample of 29 brown-headed cowbirds (Molothrus ater). Nucleotide diversity values based on data from these two different markers were almost identical (mtDNA, 0.0017; RAPDs, 0.0019). These data suggest to us that RAPDs may evolve at a similar rate to mtDNA in wild vertebrate populations. Thus, in terms of time-scales of expected rates of evolutionary change, RAPDs may represent a class of nuclear markers which evolve at a rate similar to that of mtDNA. Clearly, however, additional studies comparing the levels of variation in both kinds of markers in the same sample of organisms are required to further investigate this idea. A weakness of the method proposed by Clark & Lanigan (1993) is that estimates of genotype frequencies are based on the frequency of individuals with no frag- ments present at a particular 'locus'. This proportion is used to estimate q2 or the frequency of recessive homozy- gotes. Two problems with this way of estimating geno- type frequencies can arise. One, presence or absence of fragments in RAPD profiles is extremely sensitive to sub- tle changes in experimental conditions (e.g. Penner et al. 1993). However, experimental error in assessing indi- vidual genotypes may not have a strong effect on calcula- tions of population-level parameters so long as the repeatability of individual fragments is high. Estimates of P and D for the black rat snake populations were similar when based on either the restricted or complete data sets (Table 3). A second difficulty is that when sample sizes are small, then values for q2 estimated as described above can be extremely biased (B. Milligan, personal communi- cation), leading to inaccurate estimates of genotype fre- quencies using the Clark & Lanigan (1993) approach. This problem may be particularly acute for conservation biolo- gists who often analyse rare species from which samples are difficult to obtain. Finally, because the samples avail- able to conservation biologists in many situations are lim- ited an effort should be made to conduct a power analysis (e.g. Cohen 1988) which would explore the relationship between the detectability of population level differences m D and the number of individuals sampled and their genotypic characteristics.

Analyses with RAPD data showed no evidence fofsig- nificant differentiation between populations of black rat snakes or massasauga rattlesnakes despite the fact that both populations within each species were isolated from each other. Thus, the data tend to support the general trend suggested by electrophoretic studies on conspecific snake populations which show little genetic differentia- tion suggesting that gene flow between snake popula- tions is usually quite high (Prior, in preparation). These results need to be confirmed with data from other rap- idly-evolving genetic markers suitable for examining in- traspecific variation. We are currently exploring the use of both microsatellite markers (Queller etal. 1993) and mitochondria1 DNA sequence data as alternative sources of genetic markers for examining the level of differentia- tion between these snake populations. The lack of an effect of isolation is likely because both the black rat snake and rattlesnake populations we stud- ied were only recently separated. The Rideau Lakes and Big Creek rat snake populations probably formed part of a more-or-less continuous population which stretched 1365294x, 1994, 4, Downloaded from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-294X.1994.tb00072.x by Queen'S University, Wiley Online Library on [19/02/2023]. Given that snakes are relatively long-lived vertebrates (longevity of 15-20 years for black rat snakes and 14 years for massasauga rattlesnakes; Ernst & Barbour 1989), the genetic effects of isolation in a species with normally high levels of gene flow may take some time to appear. At minimum, however, our study has es- tablished baseline genetic data which can be used to monitor this process in the future since it is highly likely that these populations will remain isolated given the in- crease in development and, consequent habitat destruc- tion in this, the most populated region of Canada. In addition, it remains to be seen how the genetic character- istics of these isolated and reduced populations of black rat snakes compare to other contiguous populations in the USA. Similarly, it would be of interest to know how the genetic features of the extremely small relict popula- tions of massasauga rattlesnakes found in extreme south- western Ontario and the USA compare with the relatively larger Bruce Peninsula and Georgian Bay populations we studied. The genetic similarity between these snake popula- tions suggests that, at least at present, these populations are not different genetic ’stocks’. Hence, again from a strictly genetic point of view, translocation of snakes from the more abundant Rideau Lakes population to the smaller Big Creek population might be considered as a n option for increasing snake numbers in the Big Creek re- gion. However, there may be a variety of other reasons (e.g. infectious disease transmission) for not proceeding with such interpopulation transfers.
